note: Curated references behind the science page, the blog and move pages. Summaries describe what the research looked at; they are not treatment claims. Entries with verified: true come from the 2026-09-18 evidence library (PubMed + Crossref checked); quote is an exact abstract substring and the only text that may be quoted.

references.title: Breaking up prolonged sitting reduces postprandial glucose and insulin responses
references.summary: In a small lab study, adults who got up for 2-minute walks every 20 minutes had lower blood sugar and insulin after a drink than when they sat without a break.
references.authors: Dunstan, D. W., Kingwell, B. A., Larsen, R., Healy, G. N., Cerin, E., Hamilton, M. T., Shaw, J. E., Bertovic, D. A., Zimmet, P. Z., Salmon, J., & Owen, N.
references.citation: Dunstan, D. W., Kingwell, B. A., Larsen, R., Healy, G. N., Cerin, E., Hamilton, M. T., Shaw, J. E., Bertovic, D. A., Zimmet, P. Z., Salmon, J., & Owen, N. (2012). Breaking up prolonged sitting reduces postprandial glucose and insulin responses. Diabetes Care, 35(5), 976-983. https://doi.org/10.2337/dc11-1931
references.design: Randomised three-period crossover trial (acute, lab-based)
references.population: Overweight/obese adults aged 45-65 (not specifically office workers); lab simulation of a sitting day
references.keyFinding: Two-minute walking breaks every 20 min lowered post-drink glucose iAUC from 6.9 to 5.2 (light) and 4.9 (moderate) mmol/L·h, and insulin iAUC from 828.6 to about 634 pmol/L·h, versus uninterrupted sitting over 5 h.
references.quote: Interrupting sitting time with short bouts of light- or moderate-intensity walking lowers postprandial glucose and insulin levels in overweight/obese adults.

references.title: Effects of interrupting prolonged sitting with physical activity breaks on blood glucose, insulin and triacylglycerol measures: A systematic review and meta-analysis
references.summary: A 2020 review of 37 trials found that breaking up sitting with activity moderately lowered the rise in blood sugar and insulin after meals, compared with sitting still.
references.authors: Loh, R., Stamatakis, E., Folkerts, D., Allgrove, J. E., & Moir, H. J.
references.citation: Loh, R., Stamatakis, E., Folkerts, D., Allgrove, J. E., & Moir, H. J. (2020). Effects of interrupting prolonged sitting with physical activity breaks on blood glucose, insulin and triacylglycerol measures: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Medicine, 50(2), 295-330. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-019-01183-w
references.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of acute trials
references.population: Adults 18+, metabolically healthy or impaired; mostly lab studies (not specifically office workers)
references.keyFinding: Activity breaks vs continuous sitting: glucose SMD -0.54 (95% CI -0.70 to -0.37), insulin SMD -0.56 (-0.74 to -0.38), triglycerides SMD -0.26 (-0.44 to -0.09). Larger glucose effect with higher BMI. Possible publication bias for triglycerides.
references.quote: The use of PA breaks during sitting moderately attenuated post-prandial glucose, insulin, and TAG, with greater glycaemic attenuation in people with higher BMI.

references.title: Breaking up prolonged sitting reduces resting blood pressure in overweight/obese adults
references.summary: In a small one-day lab study, short walking breaks every 20 minutes were linked to slightly lower resting blood pressure (about 2-3 mmHg) than sitting all day.
references.authors: Larsen, R. N., Kingwell, B. A., Sethi, P., Cerin, E., Owen, N., & Dunstan, D. W.
references.citation: Larsen, R. N., Kingwell, B. A., Sethi, P., Cerin, E., Owen, N., & Dunstan, D. W. (2014). Breaking up prolonged sitting reduces resting blood pressure in overweight/obese adults. Nutrition, Metabolism and Cardiovascular Diseases, 24(9), 976-982. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.numecd.2014.04.011
references.design: Randomised three-treatment crossover trial (acute, lab-based)
references.population: Overweight/obese adults aged 45-65 (same cohort as Dunstan 2012); not specifically office workers
references.keyFinding: With 2-min walking breaks every 20 min, systolic BP averaged 120 (light) and 121 (moderate) vs 123 mmHg sitting; diastolic 76 and 77 vs 79 mmHg. No difference in mean arterial pressure or heart rate.
references.quote: Regularly breaking up prolonged sitting may reduce systolic and diastolic blood pressure.

references.title: Breaks in sedentary time: Beneficial associations with metabolic risk
references.summary: A landmark 2008 study found that people who broke up their sitting more often had healthier waistlines and blood markers, even with the same total sitting time.
references.authors: Healy, G. N., Dunstan, D. W., Salmon, J., Cerin, E., Shaw, J. E., Zimmet, P. Z., & Owen, N.
references.citation: Healy, G. N., Dunstan, D. W., Salmon, J., Cerin, E., Shaw, J. E., Zimmet, P. Z., & Owen, N. (2008). Breaks in sedentary time: Beneficial associations with metabolic risk. Diabetes Care, 31(4), 661-666. https://doi.org/10.2337/dc07-2046
references.design: Cross-sectional observational study (accelerometer-measured)
references.population: Australian adults from the AusDiab study, mean age 53.4 (general population, not only desk workers)
references.keyFinding: Independent of total sedentary time and MVPA, more breaks in sedentary time were associated with smaller waist circumference (beta -0.16), lower BMI (-0.19), triglycerides (-0.18) and 2-h plasma glucose (-0.18).
references.quote: This study provides evidence of the importance of avoiding prolonged uninterrupted periods of sedentary (primarily sitting) time.

references.title: Does physical activity attenuate, or even eliminate, the detrimental association of sitting time with mortality? A harmonised meta-analysis of data from more than 1 million men and women
references.summary: A study of over a million adults found that long daily sitting was linked to higher risk of early death mainly in people who got little physical activity; about 60-75 minutes a day of moderate activity appeared to offset that link.
references.authors: Ekelund, U., Steene-Johannessen, J., Brown, W. J., Fagerland, M. W., Owen, N., Powell, K. E., Bauman, A., Lee, I.-M., Lancet Physical Activity Series 2 Executive Committee, & Lancet Sedentary Behaviour Working Group
references.citation: Ekelund, U., Steene-Johannessen, J., Brown, W. J., Fagerland, M. W., Owen, N., Powell, K. E., Bauman, A., Lee, I.-M., Lancet Physical Activity Series 2 Executive Committee, & Lancet Sedentary Behaviour Working Group (2016). Does physical activity attenuate, or even eliminate, the detrimental association of sitting time with mortality? A harmonised meta-analysis of data from more than 1 million men and women. The Lancet, 388(10051), 1302-1310. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(16)30370-1
references.design: Systematic review and harmonised meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies
references.population: General adult population (16 cohorts); not specific to office workers
references.keyFinding: Versus the reference group (<4 h/day sitting, most active quartile), mortality was 12-59% higher in the two least active quartiles (HR up to 1.59 for <2.5 MET-h/week and >8 h/day sitting). In the most active quartile (>35.5 MET-h/week, about 60-75 min/day of moderate activity), sitting >8 h/day was not associated with higher mortality (HR 1.04, 0.99-1.10).
references.quote: High levels of moderate intensity physical activity (ie, about 60-75 min per day) seem to eliminate the increased risk of death associated with high sitting time.

references.title: Dose-response associations between accelerometry measured physical activity and sedentary time and all cause mortality: Systematic review and harmonised meta-analysis
references.summary: Studies that measured movement with wearable devices found that more activity of any intensity, including light activity, and less sedentary time were associated with lower risk of early death in middle-aged and older adults.
references.authors: Ekelund, U., Tarp, J., Steene-Johannessen, J., Hansen, B. H., Jefferis, B., Fagerland, M. W., Whincup, P., Diaz, K. M., Hooker, S. P., Chernofsky, A., Larson, M. G., Spartano, N., Vasan, R. S., Dohrn, I.-M., Hagströmer, M., Edwardson, C., Yates, T., Shiroma, E., Anderssen, S. A., & Lee, I.-M.
references.citation: Ekelund, U., Tarp, J., Steene-Johannessen, J., Hansen, B. H., Jefferis, B., Fagerland, M. W., Whincup, P., Diaz, K. M., Hooker, S. P., Chernofsky, A., Larson, M. G., Spartano, N., Vasan, R. S., Dohrn, I.-M., Hagströmer, M., Edwardson, C., Yates, T., Shiroma, E., Anderssen, S. A., & Lee, I.-M. (2019). Dose-response associations between accelerometry measured physical activity and sedentary time and all cause mortality: Systematic review and harmonised meta-analysis. BMJ, 366, Article l4570. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.l4570
references.design: Systematic review and harmonised meta-analysis of prospective cohorts (device-measured activity)
references.population: Middle-aged and older adults, mean age 62.6; not specific to office workers
references.n: 36,383 participants (8 studies); 2,149 deaths; median follow-up 5.8 years
references.keyFinding: Light physical activity: mortality HR 0.60, 0.44 and 0.38 across quarters 2-4 vs least active. Sedentary time: HR 1.28, 1.71 and 2.63 across quarters vs least sedentary.
references.quote: Higher levels of total physical activity, at any intensity, and less time spent sedentary, are associated with substantially reduced risk for premature mortality, with evidence of a non-linear dose-response pattern in middle aged and older adults.

references.title: World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour
references.summary: The World Health Organization's 2020 guidelines recommend that adults limit sedentary time, and state that some physical activity is better than none.
references.authors: Bull, F. C., Al-Ansari, S. S., Biddle, S., Borodulin, K., Buman, M. P., Cardon, G., Carty, C., Chaput, J.-P., Chastin, S., Chou, R., Dempsey, P. C., DiPietro, L., Ekelund, U., Firth, J., Friedenreich, C. M., Garcia, L., Gichu, M., Jago, R., Katzmarzyk, P. T., ... Willumsen, J. F.
references.citation: Bull, F. C., Al-Ansari, S. S., Biddle, S., Borodulin, K., Buman, M. P., Cardon, G., Carty, C., Chaput, J.-P., Chastin, S., Chou, R., Dempsey, P. C., DiPietro, L., Ekelund, U., Firth, J., Friedenreich, C. M., Garcia, L., Gichu, M., Jago, R., Katzmarzyk, P. T., ... Willumsen, J. F. (2020). World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 54(24), 1451-1462. https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2020-102955
references.design: Official guideline (WHO Guideline Development Group, evidence reviews)
references.population: All age groups, including adults
references.keyFinding: Adults: 150-300 min/week moderate or 75-150 min/week vigorous activity, plus muscle-strengthening; reducing sedentary behaviour recommended for all ages, but evidence was insufficient to set a sedentary threshold.
references.quote: They reaffirm messages that some physical activity is better than none, that more physical activity is better for optimal health outcomes and provide a new recommendation on reducing sedentary behaviours.

references.title: The sedentary office: An expert statement on the growing case for change towards better health and productivity
references.summary: An international expert statement recommends that desk workers regularly break up sitting with standing work, sit-stand desks, or short active breaks.
references.authors: Buckley, J. P., Hedge, A., Yates, T., Copeland, R. J., Loosemore, M., Hamer, M., Bradley, G., & Dunstan, D. W.
references.citation: Buckley, J. P., Hedge, A., Yates, T., Copeland, R. J., Loosemore, M., Hamer, M., Bradley, G., & Dunstan, D. W. (2015). The sedentary office: An expert statement on the growing case for change towards better health and productivity. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 49(21), 1357-1362. https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2015-094618
references.design: Expert consensus statement (evidence graded using ACSM levels)
references.population: Desk-based workers / employers
references.keyFinding: Desk-based workers should build up to 2 h/day of standing and light activity during working hours, progressing to 4 h/day. The authors note the evidence is largely observational or short-term.
references.quote: To achieve this, seated-based work should be regularly broken up with standing-based work, the use of sit-stand desks, or the taking of short active standing breaks.

references.title: Computer terminal work and the benefit of microbreaks
references.summary: A classic study of computer workers found that short microbreaks reduced reported discomfort, especially when taken every 20 minutes, without hurting productivity.
references.authors: McLean, L., Tingley, M., Scott, R. N., & Rickards, J.
references.citation: McLean, L., Tingley, M., Scott, R. N., & Rickards, J. (2001). Computer terminal work and the benefit of microbreaks. Applied Ergonomics, 32(3), 225-237. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0003-6870(00)00071-5
references.design: Randomised field study (three microbreak protocols, within-subject break vs no-break sessions)
references.population: Computer workers doing their usual keying work
references.n: Not stated in the abstract; the full text is paywalled
references.keyFinding: Microbreaks reduced perceived discomfort in all areas studied (neck, low back, shoulder, wrist/forearm), most with breaks at 20-minute intervals, with no evidence of harm to productivity.
references.quote: It was determined (p < 0.05) that microbreaks had a positive effect on reducing discomfort in all areas studied during computer terminal work, particularly when breaks were taken at 20 min intervals.

references.title: The effects of breaks on low back pain, discomfort, and work productivity in office workers: A systematic review of randomized and non-randomized controlled trials
references.summary: A systematic review of office-worker trials found moderate-quality evidence that active breaks with a change of posture can ease discomfort, and that breaks did not hurt productivity.
references.authors: Waongenngarm, P., Areerak, K., & Janwantanakul, P.
references.citation: Waongenngarm, P., Areerak, K., & Janwantanakul, P. (2018). The effects of breaks on low back pain, discomfort, and work productivity in office workers: A systematic review of randomized and non-randomized controlled trials. Applied Ergonomics, 68, 230-239. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apergo.2017.12.003
references.design: Systematic review (GRADE) of 8 RCTs and 3 non-randomised controlled trials
references.population: Office workers
references.keyFinding: Low-quality evidence of conflicting effects of breaks on pain; low-quality evidence of benefit for discomfort; moderate-quality evidence that active breaks with postural change help pain and discomfort; moderate-quality evidence of no harm to productivity.
references.quote: Moderate-quality evidence indicated that the use of breaks had no detrimental effect on work productivity.

references.title: Effects of an active break and postural shift intervention on preventing neck and low-back pain among high-risk office workers: A 3-arm cluster-randomized controlled trial
references.source: Scandinavian Journal of Work, Environment & Health
references.summary: In a 6-month trial of office workers, those prompted to take active breaks or shift posture reported new neck or low-back pain less often than a control group.
references.authors: Waongenngarm, P., van der Beek, A. J., Akkarakittichoke, N., & Janwantanakul, P.
references.citation: Waongenngarm, P., van der Beek, A. J., Akkarakittichoke, N., & Janwantanakul, P. (2021). Effects of an active break and postural shift intervention on preventing neck and low-back pain among high-risk office workers: A 3-arm cluster-randomized controlled trial. Scandinavian Journal of Work, Environment & Health, 47(4), 306-317. https://doi.org/10.5271/sjweh.3949
references.design: 3-arm cluster-randomised controlled trial, 6-month follow-up
references.population: Healthy but high-risk office workers in Bangkok, Thailand, mostly women
references.keyFinding: New neck pain over 6 months: 17% (active break) and 17% (postural shift) vs 44% (control); new low-back pain: 9% and 7% vs 33%. Adjusted HR for neck pain 0.45 (active break); for low-back pain 0.34 (active break). Confidence intervals were wide.
references.quote: Interventions to increase either active breaks or postural shifts reduced new onset of neck and low-back pain among high-risk office workers.

references.title: Effectiveness of small daily amounts of progressive resistance training for frequent neck/shoulder pain: Randomised controlled trial
references.summary: In working adults with frequent neck and shoulder pain, 2 minutes a day of elastic-band resistance exercise reduced pain intensity over 10 weeks compared with a control group.
references.authors: Andersen, L. L., Saervoll, C. A., Mortensen, O. S., Poulsen, O. M., Hannerz, H., & Zebis, M. K.
references.citation: Andersen, L. L., Saervoll, C. A., Mortensen, O. S., Poulsen, O. M., Hannerz, H., & Zebis, M. K. (2011). Effectiveness of small daily amounts of progressive resistance training for frequent neck/shoulder pain: Randomised controlled trial. Pain, 152(2), 440-446. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pain.2010.11.016
references.design: Randomised controlled trial, 10 weeks
references.population: Employed adults working at least 30 h/week with frequent neck/shoulder pain (174 women, 24 men). The abstract does not say they were office workers.
references.keyFinding: Compared with control, neck/shoulder pain fell 1.4 points (0-10 scale) with 2 min/day and 1.9 points with 12 min/day of elastic-band resistance training, 5 days/week for 10 weeks.
references.quote: In conclusion, as little as 2 minutes of daily progressive resistance training for 10 weeks results in clinically relevant reductions of pain and tenderness in healthy adults with frequent neck/shoulder symptoms.

references.title: Effects of stretching exercise training and ergonomic modifications on musculoskeletal discomforts of office workers: A randomized controlled trial
references.summary: In a 6-month trial of office workers who already had neck, shoulder or low-back discomfort, a regular stretching programme lowered pain scores more than no treatment.
references.authors: Shariat, A., Cleland, J. A., Danaee, M., Kargarfard, M., Sangelaji, B., & Tamrin, S. B. M.
references.citation: Shariat, A., Cleland, J. A., Danaee, M., Kargarfard, M., Sangelaji, B., & Tamrin, S. B. M. (2018). Effects of stretching exercise training and ergonomic modifications on musculoskeletal discomforts of office workers: A randomized controlled trial. Brazilian Journal of Physical Therapy, 22(2), 144-153. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjpt.2017.09.003
references.design: 4-arm randomised controlled trial, 6 months
references.population: Office workers aged 20-50 with neck, shoulder and low-back pain (Malaysia)
references.keyFinding: Stretching vs control reduced Cornell pain scores for the neck (MD -10.55), right shoulder (-12.17), left shoulder (-11.1) and low back (-7.8). Only the exercise group kept improving from month 4 to 6.
references.quote: To have a long term effective on MSDs, physical therapists and occupational therapists should use stretching exercises in their treatment programs rather than solely rely on ergonomic modification.
references.quoteLocation: Abstract, Conclusion (the grammatical error 'long term effective' is in the original; keep it verbatim or quote the results numbers instead)

references.title: Effectiveness of exercise in office workers with neck pain: A systematic review and meta-analysis
references.summary: A review of 8 trials in office workers with neck pain; strengthening exercise reduced pain compared with no exercise, while the effects of stretching and endurance exercise were unclear.
references.authors: Louw, S., Makwela, S., Manas, L., Meyer, L., Terblanche, D., & Brink, Y.
references.citation: Louw, S., Makwela, S., Manas, L., Meyer, L., Terblanche, D., & Brink, Y. (2017). Effectiveness of exercise in office workers with neck pain: A systematic review and meta-analysis. South African Journal of Physiotherapy, 73(1), Article 392. https://doi.org/10.4102/sajp.v73i1.392
references.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
references.population: Office workers with non-specific neck pain
references.keyFinding: Meta-analysis showed a clinically significant difference favouring strengthening exercise over no exercise for pain (not for quality of life). Only one study tested stretching.
references.quote: There is level II evidence recommending that clinicians include strengthening exercise to improve neck pain and QoL.

references.title: Workplace interventions for reducing sitting at work
references.summary: A Cochrane review found low-quality evidence that sit-stand desks reduce time spent sitting at work, and early evidence that short, frequent breaks and computer prompts can also cut sitting time.
references.authors: Shrestha, N., Kukkonen-Harjula, K. T., Verbeek, J. H., Ijaz, S., Hermans, V., & Pedisic, Z.
references.citation: Shrestha, N., Kukkonen-Harjula, K. T., Verbeek, J. H., Ijaz, S., Hermans, V., & Pedisic, Z. (2018). Workplace interventions for reducing sitting at work. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2018(12), Article CD010912. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD010912.pub5
references.design: Cochrane systematic review
references.population: Workers in sedentary occupations, high-income countries
references.keyFinding: Sit-stand desks cut workplace sitting by about 100 min/workday short-term (low-quality evidence) and 57 min medium-term. Short breaks (1-2 min every 30 min) reduced sitting by 40 min/day vs two 15-min breaks (1 study, low quality). Computer prompts plus information reduced sitting by 55 min/day at medium term (1 study).
references.quote: At present there is low-quality evidence that the use of sit-stand desks reduce workplace sitting at short-term and medium-term follow-ups.

references.title: Effectiveness of an intervention for reducing sitting time and improving health in office workers: Three arm cluster randomised controlled trial
references.summary: In a year-long trial of 756 office workers, a sit-less programme with a height-adjustable desk cut daily sitting by about an hour, and was linked to small improvements in stress and wellbeing.
references.authors: Edwardson, C. L., Biddle, S. J. H., Clemes, S. A., Davies, M. J., Dunstan, D. W., Eborall, H., Granat, M. H., Gray, L. J., Healy, G. N., Jaicim, N. B., Lawton, S., Maylor, B. D., Munir, F., Richardson, G., Yates, T., & Clarke-Cornwell, A. M.
references.citation: Edwardson, C. L., Biddle, S. J. H., Clemes, S. A., Davies, M. J., Dunstan, D. W., Eborall, H., Granat, M. H., Gray, L. J., Healy, G. N., Jaicim, N. B., Lawton, S., Maylor, B. D., Munir, F., Richardson, G., Yates, T., & Clarke-Cornwell, A. M. (2022). Effectiveness of an intervention for reducing sitting time and improving health in office workers: Three arm cluster randomised controlled trial. BMJ, 378, Article e069288. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2021-069288
references.design: 3-arm cluster randomised controlled trial, 12-month follow-up
references.population: Desk-based local government employees in the UK
references.keyFinding: At 12 months, daily sitting fell by 22.2 min/day (programme alone) and 63.7 min/day (programme plus height-adjustable desk) vs control. Both groups showed small improvements in stress, wellbeing and vigour.
references.quote: Both SWAL and SWAL plus desk were associated with a reduction in sitting time, although the addition of a height adjustable desk was found to be threefold more effective.

references.title: "Give me a break!" A systematic review and meta-analysis on the efficacy of micro-breaks for increasing well-being and performance
references.summary: A 2022 meta-analysis found that micro-breaks of 10 minutes or less gave a small boost to energy and a small reduction in fatigue.
references.authors: Albulescu, P., Macsinga, I., Rusu, A., Sulea, C., Bodnaru, A., & Tulbure, B. T.
references.citation: Albulescu, P., Macsinga, I., Rusu, A., Sulea, C., Bodnaru, A., & Tulbure, B. T. (2022). "Give me a break!" A systematic review and meta-analysis on the efficacy of micro-breaks for increasing well-being and performance. PLOS ONE, 17(8), Article e0272460. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0272460
references.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of experimental and quasi-experimental studies
references.population: Mixed: workers and students (not only desk workers)
references.keyFinding: Micro-breaks (10 min or less) boosted vigour (d = 0.36) and reduced fatigue (d = 0.35), both small effects. No significant effect on overall performance (d = 0.16); benefits for performance only on less cognitively demanding tasks.
references.quote: Overall, the data support the role of micro-breaks for well-being, while for performance, recovering from highly depleting tasks may need more than 10-minute breaks.

references.title: The effects of breaks on digital eye strain, dry eye and binocular vision: Testing the 20-20-20 rule
references.summary: In a small study, computer users reminded to follow the 20-20-20 rule reported less eye strain and dryness during the reminder period; whether the improvement lasted afterwards was unclear.
references.authors: Talens-Estarelles, C., Cerviño, A., García-Lázaro, S., Fogelton, A., Sheppard, A., & Wolffsohn, J. S.
references.citation: Talens-Estarelles, C., Cerviño, A., García-Lázaro, S., Fogelton, A., Sheppard, A., & Wolffsohn, J. S. (2023). The effects of breaks on digital eye strain, dry eye and binocular vision: Testing the 20-20-20 rule. Contact Lens and Anterior Eye, 46(2), Article 101744. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.clae.2022.101744
references.design: Pre-post intervention study, no control group (2 weeks of software reminders, then 1-week washout)
references.population: Symptomatic computer users
references.keyFinding: With 20-20-20 break reminders, users took more breaks, and digital eye strain and dry eye symptoms decreased (p <= 0.045). The improvement was gone one week after the reminders stopped. No change in tear film or ocular surface signs.
references.quote: The 20-20-20 rule is an effective strategy for reducing DES and dry eye symptoms, although 2 weeks was not enough to considerably improve binocular vision or dry eye signs.

references.title: Effect of breathwork on stress and mental health: A meta-analysis of randomised-controlled trials
references.summary: A 2023 meta-analysis of randomised trials found that structured breathing practices were linked to modestly lower self-reported stress.
references.authors: Fincham, G. W., Strauss, C., Montero-Marin, J., & Cavanagh, K.
references.citation: Fincham, G. W., Strauss, C., Montero-Marin, J., & Cavanagh, K. (2023). Effect of breathwork on stress and mental health: A meta-analysis of randomised-controlled trials. Scientific Reports, 13(1), Article 432. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-27247-y
references.design: Meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
references.population: Adults (general, not workplace-specific)
references.keyFinding: Breathwork was associated with lower self-reported stress than controls (g = -0.35, small-to-medium), with similar effects for anxiety (g = -0.32) and depressive symptoms (g = -0.40). Most studies were at moderate risk of bias.
references.quote: Overall, results showed that breathwork may be effective for improving stress and mental health.

references.title: Using computer, mobile and wearable technology enhanced interventions to reduce sedentary behaviour: A systematic review and meta-analysis
references.source: International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity
references.summary: A review of 17 trials found that apps, prompting software and wearables helped people sit about 40 minutes less per day in the short term, though the effect faded over time.
references.authors: Stephenson, A., McDonough, S. M., Murphy, M. H., Nugent, C. D., & Mair, J. L.
references.citation: Stephenson, A., McDonough, S. M., Murphy, M. H., Nugent, C. D., & Mair, J. L. (2017). Using computer, mobile and wearable technology enhanced interventions to reduce sedentary behaviour: A systematic review and meta-analysis. International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity, 14(1), Article 105. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12966-017-0561-4
references.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
references.population: Healthy adults (includes but is not limited to office workers)
references.keyFinding: Technology-based interventions (apps, prompting software, wearables) reduced sitting by 41 min/day on average. Effects were 42 min/day short-term but only 1.7 min/day beyond 6 months. 'Prompts and cues' was among the most common behaviour-change techniques. 16 of 17 studies had high or unclear risk of bias.
references.quote: Effectiveness appeared most prominent in the short-term and lessened over time.

references.title: Effectiveness of workplace interventions in the prevention of upper extremity musculoskeletal disorders and symptoms: an update of the evidence
references.summary: A systematic review finding strong evidence that workplace resistance training, and moderate evidence that stretching programmes, can help prevent and manage upper-limb musculoskeletal symptoms.

references.title: "Sit Up Straight": time to re-evaluate
references.source: Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy
references.summary: An editorial reviewing evidence that no single sitting posture prevents pain, and that changing position and moving regularly matters more than holding a 'correct' posture.

references.title: How breath-control can change your life: a systematic review on psycho-physiological correlates of slow breathing
references.summary: A systematic review associating slow breathing techniques with increased parasympathetic activity and reports of relaxation and reduced anxiety in healthy adults.

references.title: Digital eye strain: prevalence, measurement and amelioration
references.summary: A review of digital eye strain in screen users, discussing regular breaks from near work, blinking and distance viewing among the practical measures.
